item.title: Okinawa Diving & Snorkelling Guide: Spots, Trips & Tips
item.description: With warm, gin-clear seas, vast coral reefs and abundant marine life, Okinawa is one of Asia’s great diving and snorkelling destinations. From the dazzling “Kerama Blue” reefs and the glowing Blue Cave off Cape Maeda, to manta cleaning stations and the mysterious Yonaguni Monument, there’s something for every level — including easy trial (“experience”) dives for total beginners and snorkelling trips for non-divers. Operators across the island make it simple to get in the water.

item.title: Sea Turtle Snorkelling Guide: Zamami & Okinawa Tours
item.description: Swimming alongside a wild green sea turtle in Okinawa’s crystal water is a bucket-list moment — and surprisingly attainable. The reefs around Zamami in the Kerama Islands are among the best places in Japan to snorkel with sea turtles, which graze on seagrass close to shore and surface for air right beside swimmers. With easy beach-entry spots and guided tours that know where the turtles feed, it’s an experience open to families and casual snorkellers, not just divers.

item.title: Diving & Snorkelling in Okinawa: Complete 2026 Guide
item.description: Okinawa is Japan’s diving capital — and for good reason. The Ryukyu archipelago stretches 1,200 km from the main island to Yonaguni on the Taiwan border, encompassing some of the most diverse marine environments in the North Pacific: from shallow coral gardens with sea turtles to deep-water hammerhead shark schools, WWII wrecks, and the infamous “Yonaguni Monument” (an underwater rock formation that may or may not be man-made). Is Okinawa Good for Non-Divers?

item.title: Kerama Islands & Okinawa Coral Reefs: The Complete Guide
item.description: The Kerama Islands — 30 km west of Naha — contain some of the most pristine coral reefs in East Asia. Marine biologists have recorded over 250 species of coral and 360 species of fish in the Kerama Shoto National Park. The water clarity here — what the Japanese call “Kerama Blue” (ケラマブルー) — is the result of both the Kuroshio Current and the absence of agricultural runoff on these small uninhabited or lightly populated islands.
